The Guitalculator

a small suite of guitar-setup calculators · offline · presets stay on this machine

OverCompensator2000
Works out exactly where to cut the saddle and (optionally) the nut so every fretted note plays in tune, string by string — accounting for gauge, tension, action height, and how far a real finger stretches the string sharp.
⇆ String count, gauges, and nut width stay in sync with the NutBuster64 tab automatically, both directions — no button to press.

PresetsⓘClick a preset's name to load it, or the × to delete it. Presets are saved to this browser (in inches internally). Use Export/Import to move a string-set library between computers or back it up.

Commercial String SetsⓘPicking an instrument below fills typical gauges, materials and pitches immediately — everything stays fully editable, these are starting points, not gospel. Every entry is an estimate unless a real named set is available below (look for the ⚠/✓ markers). Named sets pull the exact published gauges and unit weights from the manufacturer's own library — not an approximation; pitch/action still come from the typical instrument profile.

Common Parameters

Old Guitar ModeⓘHave a real, already-built instrument? Enter its existing saddle position and check whether the ideal compensation actually fits it.
—

Multiscale (fanned-fret)ⓘDifferent scale length per side, fanning from a pivot fret.

Disabled while Old Guitar Mode is on — an existing, already-built instrument has one real, fixed nut/saddle geometry, not a per-string fanned one this app can measure. Turn Old Guitar Mode off above to use Multiscale.

How multiscale is seeded & drawnⓘScale length is per-string, interpolated linearly from string 1 to the last string, exactly like the existing per-string Scale (L) column — the physics doesn't change, only how it's seeded. Perpendicular fret only affects the diagram below (where the fan visually pivots); it doesn't change any compensation number.

Mandolin / 12-String ModeⓘSet up paired or tripled courses instead of individual strings — same idea as Mandolin/12-String Mode over in NutBuster64. Also unlocks staggered per-course saddle/nut options in the Nut & Saddle Diagrams section.

Changing either field rebuilds the string list to match (e.g. 4 courses × pair = 8 strings, course 1 = strings 1–2, course 2 = strings 3–4, etc). Every string still gets its own individual scale/pitch/gauge/action/compensation — a unison pair needs identical values on both strings, an octave pair needs different ones — edit each row after. The results table and diagrams group by course automatically.

The real physical gap between the strings within one course (typically .078″–.109″ / 2.0–2.8mm) — used only to work out each string's tiny real offset from its course's fan position, same idea as NutBuster64's own Intra-Course Spacing field but set independently here.

String Parametersⓘ Sources. The two underlying terms — a stretch term (a12²·E·S / T·L) and a bending-stiffness term (2√(E·I/T)), with S=(π/4)d² and I=(π/64)d⁴ — come from Sjaak Elmendorp's published equations in "It's All About the Core, or How to Estimate Compensation," American Lutherie #104 (2010), freely available via the Guild of American Luthiers (luth.org). Hex cores get S×1.10 / I×1.20 per Elmendorp's own correction.

How the two terms combine, and core diameter, were reverse-engineered against Mottola's real calculator, not published anywhere. Elmendorp's own article adds the two terms directly, matching his own worked example almost exactly. Mottola's calculator combines them in quadrature, √(stretch²+bending²), instead — this app uses Mottola's variant, since it's the more widely-used reference, with wound-steel core diameter estimated as 0.0091 + 0.162×overall (inches), fitted to real string-by-string values from Mottola's output. Lands within 0–2% of Mottola's numbers on 4 of 6 strings tested, 7–12% on the other two. A fit to a handful of data points, not a closed-form match.

Nut compensation (Simple mode) is Gore's own published 50/50 split of the saddle-only total. Advanced mode jointly solves nut AND saddle compensation together from Gore's own full per-fret physical model (Sec. 4.7.3, Equ. 4.7-11 through 4.7-37) — see the "?" button next to the Advanced method dropdown for the full derivation.

String data in the library is pulled from manufacturers' own technical documents: D'Addario's Catalog Supplement / String Tension Specifications (393 entries) and GHS's Electric and Acoustic Guitar String Guides (78 entries). Ernie Ball doesn't publish unit weight data. Core diameter for wound strings is still an estimate (per the fitted formula above) since neither brand publishes it — it only affects the stretch/bending math, not tension.

"Straight?" columnⓘWhether this string counts toward the straight-saddle calculation (the single, uncompensated-per-string saddle line shown further down and used for the "Total Scale Length" figure). Most acoustic and classical guitars use one straight saddle, not a separately shaped/stepped one for every string, so most builders fit that single straight line to look best across the strings they actually care about — leave this checked for strings you want included in that fit. Uncheck it for a string you plan to compensate individually instead (the B string is the classic example on steel-string guitars, along with G on classical), or for a very low string where pitch differences are harder to hear anyway.

Straight-saddle values use linear regression, restricted to strings marked "Straight?".ⓘStraight-saddle values use simple linear regression of each string's individual compensation across position, restricted to strings marked "Straight?" — uncheck a string (e.g. a separately-compensated B string) to exclude it and tighten the fit for the rest. With Split Saddle on, each segment gets its own independent fit using only the strings assigned to it.

Nut & Saddle DiagramsⓘStraight-sided blanks (bone/plastic nuts and saddles are cut straight; compensation comes from where each string breaks along the top, not from shaping the footprint). The saddle band is fitted through each string's actual required position. The nut band is different: its front edge (the bridge-facing side, drawn on the right in the mirrored nut panel) is fixed flush at whichever string's break point sits furthest forward (toward the bridge) — the string with the LARGEST nut compensation, since positive nut compensation moves the nut forward, shortening the open string — accounting for the multiscale fan angle. That string sits at exactly 0.000 setback (or all of them, if more than one ties), and every other string is cut back from there. This is a real physical constraint, not an arbitrary pick: every slot needs nut material under it, so the front edge has to reach the most-forward one. With positive compensation that edge sits forward of the theoretical zero fret, so the fingerboard has to stop short of that line to make room. Both axes use the same real-unit scale — string spacing (vertical) uses the nut width / bridge spacing settings in the Fretboard Diagram card, so the saddle and nut are drawn genuinely long and thin, the way a real one is, not stretched to fill the panel. The nut panel only appears when Nut Compensation is switched on above; if multiscale is on, both diagrams' fan angle reflects the real fanned-fret geometry. ▲/▼ on the nut/saddle width fields above (or the nut width in the Fretboard Diagram card, for the fingerboard span used for string spacing) move by exactly 0.1mm (or its inch equivalent) every time, or just enter your desired value; press Enter to apply a change (these don't recalculate on every keystroke). With Split Saddle on, check "start a new saddle segment" for a string in the String Parameters table above — that string and everything below it move to a new independent segment, common for a stepped/broken saddle where, say, the B string and everything below it sit on a separately-angled piece.

Split saddle
A "broken" saddle — fit an independent straight line to each segment instead of one line for every string. Adjust where each segment starts in the String Parameters table above.
Vertical saddle (parallel to nut)
Force a flat, unangled saddle at the best average position, instead of an angled best-fit line — some strings may fall outside it
Staggered saddle (per-course)
Mandolin/12-String Mode only — instead of one straight/angled line for every string, fit each course its own independent little segment, closer to how an adjustable mandolin or 12-string bridge is really built. Overrides Split Saddle when on.

Sane defaults filled in for all four — all four now feed the Advanced calculation's per-fret action model directly — see the "?" button above for exactly how.ⓘFinger depression: how far your fretting finger displaces the string past the fret (Gore's stated realistic typical ~0.3mm/0.012in) — the strongest driver of the three; a harder fretting hand nudges saddle compensation up noticeably. Nut height (typical minimum ~0.1mm/0.004in) and neck relief at fret 7 (typical ~0.1–0.2mm/0.004–0.008in) both set the string's height-above-fret curve (Equ. 4.7-11 to 4.7-22) that the saddle solve runs on, so they do move the result too, just more mildly than finger depression.

All four of these feed the Optimized (Price) calculation directly (it builds a full per-fret action curve from them) — see the "?" button above for exactly how.

Nut & Saddle Compensation — Full Cutting Detail (Simple)ⓘEverything for actually cutting the nut and saddle with whichever method is currently selected above, all in one box: the nut compensation measured from all three reference points (theoretical zero / 1st fret / 12th fret), the saddle compensation measured from the two reference points that are actually practical on the saddle side (theoretical zero / 12th fret — the 1st fret is omitted here since on the saddle side it's nearly a full scale length away, not something you'd actually measure to), and a new "Total length" column — the real physical distance from the nut's own (compensated) face to the saddle's own (compensated) face. That last column is NOT the same thing as the Results table's "Total Scale Length" column above: that one is scale + saddle comp. only, deliberately ignoring the nut's position entirely, because nut position has no effect on fretted-note intonation (it's the acoustic/vibrating length). This "Total length" column is the literal nut-face-to-saddle-face gap you'd measure with calipers after both ends are cut: scale − nut comp. + saddle comp. — positive nut compensation moves the nut toward the saddle (shortening that gap), positive saddle compensation moves the saddle away from the nut (lengthening it). This box always tracks whichever method is selected in the Method dropdown above; switch methods and it updates. In Old Guitar Mode, the saddle numbers are the real, fixed saddle position regardless of method.

"Zero" is the raw Nut Comp./Saddle Comp. value for the currently-selected method (the same numbers the Results table above shows). Positive nut compensation moves the nut face forward, toward the frets, so the nut's "1st fret" and "12th fret" columns are that fret's fixed distance from the theoretical zero minus Nut Comp. (shorter than the uncompensated ref.); positive saddle compensation moves the saddle away from the frets, so the saddle's "12th fret" column is half the scale length plus Saddle Comp. The three comparison boxes below use the same rule. The new "Uncompensated ref." columns show that same fixed distance ALONE, with zero compensation added -- i.e. where the 1st/12th fret would sit if the nut and saddle were still exactly at the theoretical zero-fret point -- so you can see at a glance how much the selected method's own numbers actually differ from that baseline (there's no "Zero" baseline column since by definition that distance is always zero). See the "?" above for what "Total length" means and how it differs from the Results table's "Total Scale Length".

Nut Compensation: Distance to Nut Face, by Method and by Reference PointⓘThree boxes below, one per reference point (theoretical zero / 1st fret / 12th fret — the same three real, markable points the "Measure compensation from" selector above uses for the diagrams), each showing what Simple, Advanced, Optimized (Price), and Byers would each put on the NUT for every string, side by side, measured from that reference point back to the nut face. Useful for seeing how much the choice of method actually matters for your specific setup before committing to one, from whichever real point you'd actually hold a ruler or calipers against. The currently-selected method's column is highlighted in all three boxes. In Old Guitar Mode, all four methods collapse to the same number (whatever the fixed saddle position doesn't already cover), since the saddle isn't free to move in any of them.

All values are distances back to the nut face, in the unit currently selected above. "From theoretical zero" is each method's raw Nut Comp. value (the same number the Results table's own Nut Comp. column shows): how far the nut face sits forward of the theoretical zero line, toward the bridge (negative = behind it). "From 1st fret" and "from 12th fret" are that real fret's own fixed distance from the theoretical zero minus the method's Nut Comp., since moving the nut face toward the bridge brings it closer to every fret — so these three boxes are the same three underlying method values, just measured from three different starting points — not three different calculations. The "Uncomp. ref." column in the 1st-fret and 12th-fret boxes shows that same fixed distance by itself, with no compensation applied — i.e. where that fret would measure to if the nut were still sitting exactly at the theoretical zero-fret point — so you can see at a glance how far each method's own column has actually moved it from that baseline (there's no equivalent column in the "from theoretical zero" box, since that baseline distance is zero by definition there).

Optimized (Price)'s column looks unrelated to the other two on purpose, not by mistake: Simple and Advanced both work by splitting one shared total (a fraction of it goes to the nut, the rest to the saddle), so their nut numbers scale up and down with each string the same way the saddle numbers do. Price's nut number is a completely different kind of quantity — a single small constant shared by the whole nut (often negative), from his own published data, that only fine-tunes the OPEN string and never subtracts from the saddle setback. It's the SAME number on every string, including on a fanned/multiscale instrument (it's derived from the instrument's average scale length, not each string's own fanned scale) — if you see it trending smoothly up or down string-by-string instead of sitting flat, that would be a bug, not this deliberate design. Check the Saddle Comp. column instead (in the Results table above) if you want to sanity-check Price against the other two — those line up closely, since they're solving the same fretted-note problem. See the Optimized (Price) method's own info box above for the full explanation.

Byers' column is real measured data for one specific guitar (Gregory Byers' own 650mm-scale classical, strung with Augustine Regal), not a from-scratch calculation like Simple/Advanced, or a scale-only constant like Price — it's a different, genuinely per-string value for each of the 6 strings (nut moved toward the saddle by Byers' own measured set-forth), scaled proportionally to your own instrument's scale length. It only ever shows real numbers for exactly 6 strings (a dash otherwise) — there's no principled way to extend his measured 6-string data to a 7-string, 12-string, or other instrument. See the Byers method's own info box above for the full source, derivation, and honest limits.

Calculate even nut spacing for up to 13 strings, accounting for actual string gauge — in inches and millimeters at once.

Setup

Pick this first — it changes what "nut width" even means for everything below. New Guitar flips the calculation around: instead of entering a nut width and seeing where the strings land, enter the string spacing you actually want (Equal Gaps or Equal Centers, set below) plus the edge distances, and this works out the ideal nut width for you, then drives every other number on this tab and OverCompensator2000's from that — a genuinely different set of numbers than starting from a width. Existing Nut Width is the original flow: you already know (or have measured) the nut width, so you enter it directly below.

Switch anytime — your numbers convert automatically, and results always show both units.

The gap you want between adjacent string surfaces (edge to edge), same idea as Equal Gaps mode below, just solved in the opposite direction. Defaults to the gap worked out from a normal Fender Telecaster's own nut width (see the hint below the computed width for the source numbers) — edit freely for your own instrument.

String count, gauges, and nut width always stay in sync with the Saddle Compensation tab automatically, both ways — no toggle needed.

The exact same string library (D'Addario, GHS, Savarez, Hannabach, La Bella — real published gauges) used by OverCompensator2000's own string picker, so you don't have to type gauges in twice or keep the two tabs in sync by hand.

Presets

Click a preset's name to load it (sets string/course count, gauges, nut width, edge distance, and mode all at once), or the × to delete it — that includes the built-in starter sets, so delete anything you don't need. Presets save to this browser automatically. Use Export/Import to move them between computers or back them up.

Turns each string into a paired course — set how far apart the two strings in a pair sit, and how far apart the pairs themselves sit.

Set scale lengths here, or on the OverCompensator2000 tab — either way both tabs stay in sync automatically and fan the nut/bridge diagrams and tables to match, instead of drawing them straight across.

Mandolin = 4 courses (8 strings). 12-string guitar = 6 courses (12 strings). Up to 8 courses (16 strings) supported.

Edge distance is measured from the fingerboard edge to the center of the outermost string. By default the same distance is used on both sides. Fill in "Bass Side" only if the low/bass string (the last, thickest one) needs a different offset than the treble side above. Tip: you can paste messy text into Nut Width or Edge Distance (like "Nut width: 43mm") and it'll pull out just the number.

"Straight across" is the plain across-the-neck span (perpendicular to the centerline) — the number synced to the rest of this app and to OverCompensator2000. "Along the face" is the real length of the nut blank itself, measured square to its own front edge — only different from the straight-across number when Multiscale Mode is on and the nut is actually cut at an angle; otherwise the two match. The Desired Gap field above defaults to 0.2383" (6.05mm) — the Equal-Gaps spacing this app's own math works out for a 1.650" nut width, the commonly-published classic/standard Fender Telecaster spec (modern wide-neck Fender models use 1.685" instead), with this app's own default string gauges (.010–.046) and edge distance. Edit any of those and this number stops being Telecaster-specific, which is expected.

Same idea as the nut fields above, but for the Bridge Diagram below — a real bridge/saddle is almost always wider than the nut, with its own edge distances, using the same string count and gauges. The default width (2.430", with the 0.172" edge distance above, works out to a 2.086" outer-string spread) matches the commonly-published vintage/standard Fender 6-saddle bridge spacing — edit freely for your own bridge.

How far the fingerboard's own edge extends past the outermost string's centerline at the 12th fret — there's no fixed industry "standard" for this the way there is for the geometry below it, it's a build/design choice, so this just defaults to the average of your nut and bridge edge margins above and is fully editable.

The 12th fret sits at exactly the midpoint of every string's own scale length (2−12/12 = 0.5 exactly, true for straight and fanned/multiscale necks alike, and for every string individually even when scale lengths differ), so the string spread there is exactly the average of the nut spread and the bridge spread above — a real geometric fact, not an approximation. Total width then adds the edge margin (both sides) from the field above. With the defaults as shipped (Telecaster-style nut spacing, Telecaster-style bridge spacing), this works out to roughly what a real Telecaster's fingerboard measures at the 12th fret.

Equal Gaps compensates for string thickness so the gap between string surfaces is identical. Recommended for most instruments.

Gauges

Gauge = the string's actual diameter, in in. E.g. a plain .010" high-E, or a wound .046" low-E.

Course Spacing & Gauges

Most mandolins and 12-strings use pairs. Triple courses show up on some 9/12-course mandolins, Portuguese guitarra, and similar instruments.

Pair Gap keeps the same physical gap between neighboring strings of every course, adjusting for each course's own gauges. Pair Centers keeps a fixed center-to-center distance regardless of gauge.

Typical mandolin/12-string intra-course spacing is about .078"–.109" (2.0–2.8mm). For triple courses, this same spacing is used between each neighboring pair within the course.

Enter both string gauges for each course. Unison pairs use the same gauge twice; octave pairs (common on the wound bass courses) use two different gauges.

Paste anything — a clean list, or messy text with labels like "String 1:", product names, or prices mixed in. We'll ignore the noise and pull out whatever looks like real gauges. By default we sort thinnest to thickest (string 1 = thinnest); check the box above if you're pasting mandolin or 12-string course pairs (like an octave pair ".023 .009") and need to keep them exactly in the order you pasted, so paired strings stay adjacent. Then name and save it as a preset above.

Wired!
The Guitar Wirer — choose your pickups, controls and switches, say what each switch position should do, and the wiring is worked out for you, checked in every switch setting, and drawn as a diagram with build steps.

Result

Wiring diagram

What each switch setting does

Build steps

Honest limits

The circuit is worked out and re-checked for every combination of switch positions, so what the table says is what the wiring does. What it can't know: your exact switch's lug numbering (check the datasheet), pickup colour codes that a maker has changed, and how things sound beyond level, phase and hum. The settings table assumes every pot is on 10; the tone graph lets you turn them, but it uses typical published pickup values (inductance, winding capacitance), so read it as a comparison, not a measurement. Active pickups and on-board buffers/preamps get their battery switched by a stereo jack's ring; a preamp is modelled as a clean, flat gain stage (no EQ). Free-Way 3X3-03 and 3X3-05 are built in from Free-Way's own schematics; other Free-Way models need their contact table entered.

Old drag-and-drop board (superseded — it wires tone pots in series with the signal, which is wrong; kept only for reference)

Preset

Loads components already placed and wired — drag anything around or rewire it afterward, nothing is locked.

InstrumentⓘGuitar vs. Bass changes which pickup types and pot values the palette offers. Acoustic assumes a piezo/preamp system rather than magnetic pickups.

ComponentsⓘSet the type/value here before dragging if you already know it — every placed component also has its own gear icon to change type/value/manufacturer afterward, and a red × to remove it.

Drag a card onto the board. Limits: 4 pickups, 5 pots, 4 switches, 2 jacks.

Hover (or tap) a component above for a close-up.

Pickups drop into one of the four locked positions on the left (Neck through Bridge) — pick each one's function from its own dropdown. Pots, switches, and jacks drop anywhere in the grid on the right, and can be dragged to reorder them. Drag from a pickup's single output dot to a switch input or a pot's input lug to link it — that's the only wire you draw by hand; everything else (which leads to splice, where the grounds go) is filled in automatically once you click "Wire it". A wire already attached to a terminal can be dragged to a different terminal to move it, or into empty space to disconnect it; click any wire to light it up, then press Delete to remove it. Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) undoes the last change on this board, step by step; Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y redoes it. Hover (or tap) a component for a close-up below the board.

Connections

Wiring diagramⓘA separate, print-style diagram -- pickups run top-to-bottom in real neck-to-bridge order, drawn as real pictorial parts (a coil, a lugged pot, a lugged switch, a jack barrel) with real colour-coded wires landing on each part's actual lug; each jack gets its own column, so a two-output instrument draws as two clearly separate signal paths instead of assuming there's only ever one output.

Updates automatically as you wire the board and after "Wire it" expands each pickup's function into its real leads. A dashed line is a pickup's link before "Wire it" has resolved it into real leads; a dimmed, dashed-outline lug is one that's not wired to anything yet. Hover a pot, switch, or jack for a full-sized close-up of exactly how to wire it -- a pickup shows only its selected function here, since its own full colour-coded lead list is one hover away on whatever it's wired to.

Honest limits

This gives correct, industry-published wire colors for the manufacturers listed and a real, physically-sensible set of terminals per component — but exact lug/terminal numbering varies by the specific switch or pot model you buy, and manufacturers occasionally revise their color codes between production runs. A selector switch here is simplified to labeled inputs plus a common output rather than each of its real internal poles; which pickups sum together at each position is still accurate, but treat the terminal count as a wiring guide, not a literal lug-for-lug map of your specific switch. Varitone cap values referenced in its close-up are the commonly-published Gibson ES-345/355 numbers, not a measurement of your specific unit. A pickup's own internal wiring (which leads to splice, which to ground) is generated for you from its selected function and is a correct, standard way to wire that function -- but everything downstream of that (which pot or switch input it feeds, how pots and jacks chain together) is still exactly what you dragged by hand, so an unusual circuit is still fully possible, it just isn't automated. The wiring diagram card lays components out in clean columns by role (pickups, switch, pots, jacks) purely to keep every wire traceable -- it's a schematic, not a scale drawing of where things physically sit in the guitar's cavity. Always cross-check against your actual component's datasheet before you solder.

How the Advanced nut/saddle split works

Trevor Gore's book (Contemporary Acoustic Guitar Design and Build) describes a full numerical model that solves for nut and saddle compensation, fret by fret, from first principles (how a string's path bends around a fretting finger, the resulting tension change, and so on — Sec. 4.7.3, Equ. 4.7-11 through 4.7-37). This app took three attempts to get a working version of that model; the first two are kept below as history, since the reasons they failed are worth knowing. The equations themselves turned out to be fine — the missing piece, both times, was having the complete, correctly-transcribed set of them to work from.

What Advanced mode does now

It reconstructs Gore's own per-fret model directly: the circle+ellipse+line neck-curvature model (Equ. 4.7-13 to 4.7-22), the three-segment fretted-string path length around a finger (Equ. 4.7-23 to 4.7-30), the resulting tension change (Equ. 4.7-31), and the inverted-Mersenne length a fret would need to sound exactly in tune (Equ. 4.7-32 to 4.7-35) — all evaluated from your actual scale, action, relief, nut height, string gauge and playing style, not a fit to someone else's published example.

Nut compensation and saddle compensation are then solved together, as one genuine joint fit over Equ. 4.7-37's summed per-fret error — matching what the book itself actually describes ("the sum... is minimised by varying the nut and saddle compensation, ΔsN and ΔsS"). A direct, fixed fret position doesn't depend on where the nut sits — substituting the book's own definition of fret position (measured from the compensated nut) shows that part cancels out exactly —

(L − nutComp + saddleComp) − (xn − nutComp) = L + saddleComp − xn

— but nut compensation still reaches every fretted note a second way: moving the nut changes the open string's length, so the player retunes it back to pitch by adjusting tension, and that retuned tension is shared by every fretted note on the string. That channel is weak on any single fret (well under a 1% tension change for a realistic nut shift) — but this optimizer minimizes a sum of errors across 18 or more frets at once, and a small bias nudging every one of those terms the same direction is exactly what a sum like that responds to. Solved as a real 2-parameter search (multi-start, so it isn't reporting a one-off local accident) rather than assumed away, it converges to the same answer from very different starting guesses and lands in the right ballpark against Gore's own Table 4.7-3/4.7-4 worked examples — including nut compensation legitimately exceeding saddle compensation on some strings, which matches those tables and which no 50/50-style split could ever produce.

Honest limits

Checked against Gore's own published worked examples (Tables 4.7-3/21-2 steel and 4.7-4/21-1 classical), this reproduces both saddle and nut compensation in the right ballpark with roughly the correct per-string trend, closest on the middle strings. The heaviest wound bass strings — and the classical G string, which the book's own text separately flags as showing unusually marked inharmonicity for a thick plain nylon string — are the least precise matches; exactly how much of the overall diameter is core versus wrap also isn't published for the book's own test strings. This app uses its own already-Mottola-validated string model for that split (the same diameter/wound/overall-diameter data the rest of this app already uses), so real string data entered here should track your actual guitar more closely than re-guessing the book's own unpublished test strings ever could, but it won't reproduce the book's exact millimetres on every string. Like Gore's own model, this drops string bending stiffness (his own stated conclusion: "practically zero impact" on intonation error — Sec. 4.7.3.3) and approximates longitudinal stiffness as k = E×A rather than measuring it on a physical test rig (his own Equ. 4.7-33 footnote, E = k/A, endorses this substitution when no rig is available).

Checked across every instrument and real string set this app ships, Advanced and Simple (50/50 split) usually land within a millimetre or two of each other in total — they're different models, so they're not expected to match exactly, but they shouldn't (and after this check, don't) wildly diverge either. The gap grows largest on the heaviest-gauge, longest-scale, highest-action setups (bass guitars, high-action gypsy-jazz guitars), where Gore's own published numbers also climb past 5mm total for comparable setups — not an app quirk, just what heavy strings genuinely need.

Old Guitar Mode + Nut Compensation

Gore's book covers a second scenario directly (Fig. 4.7-5: "an example of radical nut compensation required to bring this old, left-handed Gibson into tune") — an existing instrument where you're not touching the bridge, so the saddle position is fixed at whatever it already measures. Turning on both Old Guitar Mode and Nut Compensation switches this app into that mode: the saddle is pinned to the real nut-to-saddle distance you enter, and Advanced solves only for how much a new or re-cut nut needs to correct given that constraint — a 1-D search against the fixed saddle, rather than the full joint fit.

Why the nut can't simply make up the difference millimetre for millimetre (Sec. 4.7.2, Eq. 4.7-2/4.7-3): moving the nut forward flattens every fretted note by the same number of cents, while setting the saddle back does nothing to the open string, a full share at the 12th fret, and more above it. So a nut can only stand in for a mispositioned saddle on average. Simple, Optimized (Price) and Byers take their own free nut/saddle answer (a, b) as the shape of the string's sharpness, a + b·(2n/12−1), and pick the nut that minimises the summed error over the frets in use with the saddle held where it is (Eq. 4.7-5): nut = a + (b − saddle) × median(2n/12−1). For 20 frets that factor is about 0.83, not 1. A saddle that is already too far back gives a negative nut: the break point sits behind theoretical zero, toward the tuners.

Earlier attempts (history, all superseded)

1st attempt: the equations above (4.7-23 to 4.7-37) weren't available yet — the book pages with the actual formulas on them hadn't been photographed. That attempt improvised an ad hoc small-strain stretch shortcut and a hand-written cents-shift formula (deltaCentsFromComp(), still in the code, still correct — it exactly matches Equ. 4.7-2/ 4.7-3, the empirical/measured-with-a-tuner version of this method, Sec. 4.7.2.3, a different scenario from the one Advanced mode targets), fit as a joint 2-parameter least squares. 0.382in of saddle-only compensation, run through that formula, predicted about 52 cents of correction at fret 12; the raw per-fret error formula said only about 12–14 cents actually needed fixing there — roughly a 4× mismatch, and nut compensation came back negative and unstable on every string. That specific bug (the ad hoc stretch shortcut) was real; it was never actually a sign that joint solving itself was the problem.

2nd attempt: gave up reconstructing the physics and instead data-fit a nut/saddle split fraction directly against core diameter, calibrated to match Table 21-2's published totals for one real guitar (plain: nutFraction ≈ 71.8% − 14.13×coreDiameter(in); wound: ≈ 61.0% − 14.69×coreDiameter(in)). A real, working approximation for its time, but only ever as good as the one example it was fitted to, and it couldn't respond to changes in scale, action, or relief the way a true per-fret model does.

3rd attempt: reconstructed the full per-fret model, but — based on a derivation that turned out to be subtly wrong (a bracket-term bug plus underestimating how much that weak per-fret tension channel adds up over many frets) — wrongly concluded nut compensation couldn't be solved jointly with saddle, and instead sized it from the average cents error saddle-only compensation left behind. That produced a working-looking but badly wrong result: nut compensation came out barely above zero on every string, nothing like Gore's own published tables. Caught and fixed the same day, while checking the method across many strings and guitars — see the real, joint 2-parameter solve described above.

How the Optimized (Price) nut/saddle split works

This method is based on a self-published article, "Optimized Guitar Intonation" by Charlie Price, that you provided as photographed pages. Price's article makes one point the two methods above don't use: a fretted note's vibrating length runs from the fret to the saddle, so the nut's position has zero effect on any fretted note's pitch. That means the saddle can be positioned purely to get fretted notes in tune, without the nut in the picture at all — and only afterward does the nut get set, purely to fix the open string.

Saddle: minimizing total fretted-note error

For a candidate saddle setback, this app sums the absolute tuning error, in cents, at every fret from 1 up to your Number of Frets setting — absolute value so errors in opposite directions can't cancel each other out on paper, the same criterion Price's own article states directly. The raw per-fret error at each fret reuses this app's existing per-fret action model (buildActionModel() + computeFretErrorCents(), Gore's circle+ellipse+line neck-curvature construction, the same one Advanced mode's in-development third attempt above uses) purely as a per-fret error measurement — not run through deltaCentsFromComp(), the specific piece of that other attempt found to be roughly 4x off. Instead, how much a given saddle setback corrects each fret is computed the unambiguous way, directly from the definition of a cents shift: 1200·log₂(new vibrating length ÷ old vibrating length). Price's own article solves this with a general-purpose optimizer (Nelder-Mead simplex) and also lets fret placement itself move; this app only has saddle position as a free variable, and that total-error function is provably convex in saddle setback, so a golden-section search finds the same single best answer a general optimizer would.

Nut: Price's own published "optimized constant" preset

An earlier version of this section reasoned from first principles that nut compensation should equal the solved saddle setback (cancel the open string's added length by shortening it the same amount at the nut). That reasoning turned out to be wrong once the article's actual pages were available to read in full: Price's own Tables 3 and 4 show real nut compensation is not per-string and is not anywhere near the size of the saddle setback — it's one small, often-negative constant shared by the entire nut. His article gives two named variants: "fully optimized" nut compensation (each string carved individually) and "optimized constant" nut compensation (one shared value for the whole nut), and he states a clear preference for the latter in practice (his words: "I doubt that I will ever compensate the nut again using any other way than using the optimized constant nut compensation method"). His reason is that a single constant is what's actually practical to cut into a real nut, and the residual tuning error it leaves is small.

His article arrives at that constant by jointly re-optimizing fret placement, saddle position, and the nut constant together in one Nelder-Mead simplex run — which is why his real published fret positions differ slightly between the "fully optimized" and "optimized constant nut" scenarios in his Table 2. This app's frets are fixed at equal temperament, so it can't reproduce that joint optimization exactly. Rather than guess at a substitute formula, this app instead uses Price's own two published reference numbers directly as a preset, linearly interpolated/extrapolated by scale length:

24.9in scale → −0.0303in   25.4in scale → −0.0181in
(both for his reference string set: plain .012/.016, wound .024/.032/.042/.053, standard tuning)

That's what the Optimized (Price) method's Nut Comp. now shows: one shared value per string set, computed from those two points, not a per-string number and not equal to the saddle setback above.

What feeds this calculation

All four Advanced-mode inputs shown above the dropdown genuinely drive this one (unlike Advanced mode, where only Finger Depression currently moves the result): Nut Height and Neck Relief at fret 7 shape the per-fret action curve those errors are measured against, and Finger Depression plus Playing Style feed directly into each fret's raw error the same way they do in computeFretErrorCents() above.

A real bug caught and fixed during testing

A first version of this method used computeFretErrorCents() as-is, which deliberately omits bending stiffness — correctly, for the specific reason its own code comment gives (Gore's book found a fretting finger's effect on the neck-curvature model negligible). But that's a different physical effect from Simple mode's own already-validated comp = √(stretch² + stiffness²) formula, where "stiffness" is an inharmonicity-style effect from the string resisting a sharp bend at its fixed end points — present even on an open string, unrelated to finger pressure. Testing against a typical plain .012in high E string found that term is often the larger of the two, so leaving it out made this method's numbers come out several times too small — the exact same failure mode that got the in-development "third attempt" above parked. This version adds that same validated stiffness term back in at every fret before optimizing, and as a built-in self-check, its per-fret error at fret 12 alone now lands within a fraction of a percent of Simple mode's own number for the same string.

Honest limits

Finger-pressure is still modelled as a folded-in approximation rather than Price's or Gore's separately-measured geometry (see the comment above buildActionModel() in the code). This method also doesn't move fret placement the way Price's own article optimizes jointly — this app's frets stay equal-tempered — and, like Simple and Advanced mode, it computes each string's own compensation from that string's own scale length only, so in Multiscale mode it doesn't separately account for a fret's perpendicular-to-neck position the way the fanned-fret diagrams do. The nut number specifically is a straight-line interpolation between Price's own two published points and is calibrated to his reference light-gauge string set and standard tuning — treat it as a real, citable starting point rather than a from-scratch optimum for a very different gauge or tuning. This is the newest method in this app and the least externally cross-checked of the three — Simple mode is validated against a real independent calculator's output, Advanced mode against a real published worked example, and this one against the source article's own stated formulas/criterion for the saddle, the internal fret-12 self-check above, and the article's own Tables 3–4 numbers directly for the nut constant, not against a second independent reference. Worth spot-checking its numbers against Simple/Advanced on a representative string before trusting it for a real build.

References

Varieschi, G. & Gower, C., "Intonation and Compensation of Fretted String Instruments" (American Journal of Physics, 2010). Elmendorp, R., "Intonation of the Classical Guitar" (2010). How the Byers nut/saddle split works

This method is based on real intonation-testing work by luthier Gregory Byers, described on his own site (Guitars of Gregory Byers, "Intonation") and originally presented as a 1995 Guild of American Luthiers convention lecture, published as American Lutherie No. 47 (Fall 1996) and reprinted in The Big Red Book of American Lutherie, Vol. 4. Unlike every other method here, Byers' numbers don't come from a physical model or a closed-form formula — they come from a real measuring device.

How Byers actually measured this

Byers built a device with a fixed nut and saddle (their distance apart precisely measured) and a fretboard that could slide back and forth underneath the string. For each fret in turn, he slid the fretboard until that fret played exactly in tune against the open string (using an equal-tempered pitch reference), then recorded where the saddle needed to be for that one note. Doing this for every fret gives a real, physically-measured set of "where the saddle has to sit" positions for that specific string — already correct, by construction, with no modeling assumptions at all about stretch or stiffness.

Fitting that data to a usable nut/saddle position

That per-fret data set doesn't by itself tell you where to put a single, real, immovable nut and saddle — frets are cut at fixed equal-tempered positions, not wherever each string's own ideal curve would want them. Byers' solution: fit the whole per-fret measured data set, by least squares, to what he calls the canonical equation, a one-line generalization of standard equal-tempered fret placement that adds a free saddle-setback term:

Xn = Xa·2−n/12 + b

Here n is the fret number, Xn is the measured saddle-to-fret distance for that fret, and the fit solves for the two unknowns Xa (the string's own best-fit "nominal" zero-fret position/scale length) and b (saddle set-back from that nominal position — this app's saddleComp). Nut set-forth then falls out algebraically from the real measured total nut-to-saddle distance on the apparatus (call it X0): nut set-forth = X0 − (Xa + b) — the real nut-to-saddle gap minus the fitted nominal-scale-plus-saddle-setback. A negative set-forth therefore means the real gap is shorter than nominal: the nut sits forward, toward the saddle, shortening the open string (Byers: the nut is "moved forward to shorten the open string length"). That is the direction this app calls positive nutComp, so this app uses nutComp = −(nut set-forth).

What this app actually uses

This app does not reproduce Byers' measuring device, his per-fret fitting procedure, or his least-squares solver — there's no way to re-run his physical experiment from inside a browser, and nothing in the source material gives the raw per-fret measurements needed to refit it for a different string. Instead, this app uses his own already-published, already-fitted result directly, the same honest treatment Optimized (Price)'s own nut constant already gets here: a real number from a real reference setup, held onto as a preset rather than reinvented. Byers measured a 650mm-scale classical guitar strung with a set of Augustine Regal strings (blue label basses) and published this per-string table (nut set-forth / saddle set-back, both in mm):

String Nut set-forth (mm) Saddle set-back (mm)
1 — high E−0.31.3
2 — B−0.72.1
3 — G−1.03.1
4 — D−0.51.5
5 — A−0.51.7
6 — low E−0.52.9

This app scales both values for each string proportionally to the ratio of your instrument's own real scale length to Byers' 650mm reference, and otherwise uses them exactly as published — no re-fitting, no re-derivation, apart from flipping the nut sign onto this app's convention (above): his negative set-forth values become positive nutComp, i.e. the nut moves toward the saddle by 0.3–1.0mm. Byers confirms the direction himself: building it "will require cutting the fingerboard short at the nut end by about 1 mm to accommodate the nut set-forth of the G string." It's the only one of the four methods where the nut number is genuinely different per string (not one shared constant, like Price's, and not derived from the saddle number, like Simple/Advanced's 50/50-style splits).

Why this is scoped to exactly 6 strings

Byers only ever published six real numbers, for six specific strings on a specific standard-tuning classical guitar (string 1 = high E ... string 6 = low E, matching this app's own numbering). There's no principled way to invent a 7th or 8th string's own value, or to decide which of his six values a differently-strung or differently-tuned instrument's strings correspond to. Rather than guess, this method is only enabled for exactly 6 strings — anything else shows a dash and a warning instead of a number that would look real but mean nothing.

Honest limits

This method is only validated at 650mm scale — that's the one and only scale length Byers actually measured. It can be extrapolated to other scale lengths (this app scales his two values proportionally, rather than refusing to show anything away from 650mm), but that extrapolation is this app's own assumption, not something Byers' own material confirms: he never measured a second scale length to check whether his numbers actually behave that way as scale changes. The further your instrument's own scale is from 650mm, the more that extrapolation is doing the work, rather than Byers' own real measurement.

These are also real measured numbers for one specific guitar and one specific string set, not a general physical law — Byers himself notes in his own write-up that they "work reasonably well for most nylon strings but are probably a little on the high side for Savarez Alliance and various 'carbon' strings," and that results in practice vary with saddle height, left-hand pressure, and measurement precision. Treat this method as "what one very careful, real measurement found for one real guitar," not as a from-scratch calculation tailored to your specific gauge, tuning, or action the way Simple/Advanced/Price are.

References

Byers, G., "Classic Guitar Intonation" (Guild of American Luthiers, American Lutherie No. 47, p. 34, 1996; a transcript of his 1995 GAL Convention workshop; reprinted in The Big Red Book of American Lutherie, Vol. 4; an updated-graphics version is also hosted at proguitar.com/academy/guitar/intonation/byers-classical).
